additional_topics.summary: A stable splitting is a homotopy decomposition that appears after suspension, even when the original space cannot split because its cup products or attaching maps link its pieces. For CW complexes, the suspension of a product splits into the suspensions of the factors together with the suspension of their smash product; this extends inductively to products of several spaces. The geometric idea is to collapse suitable contractible cones in a reduced join, turning the space into a wedge.
additional_topics.learner_can_do: Recognize and use the equivalence Σ(X×Y) ≃ ΣX ∨ ΣY ∨ Σ(X∧Y), and explain why a splitting may only emerge after suspension.
additional_topics.game_hook: Have players manipulate a joined pair of spaces by collapsing designated cones, then assemble the resulting wedge pieces and compare the suspended product with its unsuspended, still-linked form.

additional_topics.title: The Loopspace of a Suspension
additional_topics.summary: For connected CW complexes X, the James reduced product J(X) has the weak homotopy type of the loopspace ΩΣX; in particular, ΩSⁿ⁺¹ can be modeled by J(Sⁿ). The excerpt motivates this equivalence by comparing their homology, and points to its use in understanding when suspension preserves homotopy groups and how it can fail beyond that range.
additional_topics.learner_can_do: Recognize ΩΣX as a loopspace that can be replaced, up to weak homotopy type, by the more structured space J(X), and identify the sphere case ΩSⁿ⁺¹ ≃ J(Sⁿ).
additional_topics.game_hook: Have players build and concatenate point-words in J(X), while matching each word to a continuously parametrized loop in ΣX; shrinking a letter toward the basepoint makes its loop fade away rather than vanish abruptly.

additional_topics.title: The Dold-Thom Theorem
additional_topics.summary: The infinite symmetric product SP(X) is the free commutative-monoid construction on a space, and the Dold–Thom theorem identifies its homotopy groups with ordinary integral homology: πₖSP(X) ≅ Hₖ(X; ℤ) for connected CW complexes. The proof strategy is to show these homotopy groups satisfy the properties of a homology theory, using quasi-fibrations and a Mayer–Vietoris argument, then determine the theory from its values on spheres.
additional_topics.learner_can_do: Explain why computing πₖSP(Sⁿ) and establishing homology-theory properties lets one identify πₖSP(X) with Hₖ(X; ℤ).
additional_topics.game_hook: Let players combine points into order-independent multisets and deform those configurations, using the surviving deformation classes to build and compare homology-like classes of the underlying space.

additional_topics.title: Steenrod Squares and Powers
additional_topics.summary: Steenrod squares and powers are natural cohomology operations that resemble self-cup-powers but, unlike cup products, are stable under suspension. Their operations (together with Bocksteins at odd primes) form Steenrod algebras acting on cohomology, so they impose constraints on spaces and maps. More generally, a cohomology operation is determined by its value on the fundamental class of an Eilenberg–Mac Lane space, connecting operations to cohomology of that space.
additional_topics.learner_can_do: Recognize why Steenrod operations can constrain a space’s possible cohomology, and distinguish their suspension-stable behavior from ordinary cup powers.
additional_topics.game_hook: Give players a space’s cohomology profile and let them use stable operation rules as compatibility tests, ruling out profiles or maps that violate the resulting constraints.

chapters.summary: Homotopy groups extend the fundamental group to higher dimensions: they share formal tools with homology, but are generally harder to compute because key decomposition theorems fail. They are powerful for detecting homotopy equivalences and connect to homology through the Hurewicz theorem; Eilenberg–MacLane spaces encode cohomology classes as homotopy classes of maps. The section also previews fibrations and Postnikov towers, where homotopy groups plus extra cohomological data (the k-invariants) describe a space’s homotopy type.
chapters.learner_can_do: Given a simply connected space with a first nonzero homotopy group in degree n, identify the Hurewicz theorem as the bridge relating it to the first nonzero homology group in that degree.
chapters.game_hook: Have players assemble a space’s homotopy profile in stages: use homotopy-group clues to build a Postnikov tower, then add or omit k-invariant cards to determine whether the result behaves like a product of Eilenberg–MacLane spaces.

back_matter.title: Appendix

sections.title: Topology of Cell Complexes
sections.summary: A CW complex is built in stages by attaching cells along their boundaries, with its topology controlled by how sets pull back under the characteristic maps. Subcomplexes inherit the CW structure and are closed; finite CW complexes are compact, and any compact subset of a CW complex lies inside a finite subcomplex. The excerpt also begins a criterion for recognizing CW structures, but the conditions are truncated.
sections.learner_can_do: Given a cell-attachment description, identify the skeleta and use characteristic maps to test whether a set is open or closed; recognize why compact subsets involve only finitely many cells.
sections.game_hook: Have players explore a complex cell by cell, testing candidate regions through their pullbacks to each characteristic disk, then compress any compactly contained region into a finite subcomplex.

sections.title: The Compact-Open Topology
sections.summary: The compact-open topology organizes maps by requiring compact subsets of the domain to land inside chosen open subsets of the target. For compact domains and metric targets, this agrees with uniform convergence; when the domain is locally compact, evaluation is continuous and continuous maps into a function space correspond exactly to continuous maps on the product. These facts make the topology a foundation for treating path spaces and adjoint maps in algebraic topology.
sections.learner_can_do: Given a compact domain, recognize or verify that a compact-open neighborhood of a map can be chosen inside a specified uniform-distance neighborhood, and vice versa.
sections.game_hook: Players steer a whole family of maps by placing compact “sensors” on the domain and assigning target regions, learning how local constraints on those sensors control global behavior such as uniform closeness.

sections.title: The Homotopy Extension Property
sections.summary: The homotopy extension property for a pair (X,A) is equivalent to the existence of a retraction from X×I onto X×{0}∪A×I. The hard direction is showing that this retraction works without assuming A is closed: the proof establishes that openness on the two pieces X and A×I determines openness in their union, so continuous data on those pieces can be extended via the retraction. The example warns that the subspace topology on this union matters and need not match the mapping-cylinder topology.
sections.learner_can_do: Given a retraction onto X×{0}∪A×I and compatible continuous data on X×{0} and A×I, explain why composing with the retraction yields a continuous extension over X×I.
sections.game_hook: Players route a partially specified homotopy across a space-time board: they must verify local openness at points near A before a retraction can carry the boundary data through the full cylinder.

sections.title: Simplicial CW Structures
sections.summary: An ordered Δ-complex equips each cell’s simplex with ordered vertices, with every face restriction matching the distinguished map of a lower-dimensional cell; forgetting order gives a more flexible but less product-friendly unordered version. Regular CW complexes admit Δ-complex structures, while barycentric subdivision makes an unordered Δ-complex regular, and doing it twice yields a simplicial complex. A key limitation is that Δ-complexes are generally not preserved by quotienting or attaching along simplicial maps.
sections.learner_can_do: Given a described cell structure, distinguish ordered Δ-complexes, unordered Δ-complexes, and simplicial complexes, and predict when barycentric subdivision is needed to reach a simplicial complex.
sections.game_hook: Have players repair a cell complex by choosing vertex orderings and subdivision moves, while navigating constraints that products favor orderings and quotient/attachment moves may break the Δ-complex structure.

back_matter.summary: A CW complex is built skeletally by attaching cells, with its topology controlled by characteristic maps from disks. Subcomplexes inherit the same topology and are closed; finite CW complexes are compact, and any compact subset lies inside a finite subcomplex. The excerpt also begins characterizing CW structures through conditions on their cells and attaching maps, but that characterization is cut off.
back_matter.learner_can_do: Given a compact subset of a CW complex, recognize that it can be contained in a finite subcomplex, and explain how characteristic maps determine the topology.
back_matter.game_hook: Have players explore a cell-built world through disk-shaped portals, testing whether local observations determine openness and gathering every region touched by a compact expedition into a finite network of cells.
